subject: maths
title: Chapter 2 · Test 2
summary: Chapter 2 test 2: parallel lines, triangle angle sums, quadrilateral properties, and interior and exterior angles of polygons.
body: This test covers Chapter 2: angles and parallel lines, angle sums of triangles, properties of quadrilaterals, interior angles of polygons and exterior angles. It has 15 questions, from easy to challenge. Allow about 25 minutes. Work with no notes and no calculator unless the question says. Diagrams are drawn to scale, but always use the angle rules and the facts you are given — never measure. Write your working, give a reason for each step, and check that your answer is the angle the question asks for (not just the value of x).

questions.prompt: AB ∥ CD and ∠APQ = 63°. Find x, the size of ∠PQC, in the diagram.
questions.explanation: x and 63° are between the parallel lines on the same side of the transversal, so they are co-interior and add to 180°: x = 117. Making them equal (63) treats them as alternate angles.
steps: Both angles are between AB and CD, on the same side (left) of PQ — co-interior angles (C shape).
Co-interior angles on parallel lines add to 180°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: these angles are co-interior (C shape), so they add to 180° — they are not equal.
mistakes.C: Step 2: co-interior angles add to 180°, not 90°.
mistakes.D: Step 2: co-interior angles add to 180°, not 360°.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines AB and CD cut by a transversal at P and Q. Angle APQ is 63° and angle CQP, on the same side of the transversal between the lines, is marked x

questions.prompt: Triangle ABC has a right angle at B and ∠A = 38°. Find x.
questions.explanation: The angles add to 180°, so x = 180 − 90 − 38 = 52. 142 forgets to subtract the right angle.
steps: The angles of a triangle add to 180°, and the square mark at B means 90°.
The two known angles add to 90 + 38 = 128.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you also need to subtract the 90° right angle, not just 38°.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 90 + 38 = 128 is the two known angles together. Subtract this from 180.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the triangle is not isosceles, so x does not have to equal 38°. Use the angle sum.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with a right angle marked at B, angle A = 38°, and the angle at C marked x

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a polygon with 11 sides. Find the sum of its interior angles.
questions.explanation: An 11-sided polygon splits into 11 − 2 = 9 triangles from one vertex, so its angle sum is 9 × 180 = 1620°. 1980° uses 11 triangles instead of 9.
steps: From one vertex it splits into 11 − 2 = 9 triangles.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the number of triangles is n − 2 = 9, not n = 11.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the number of triangles is n − 2 = 9, not n − 1 = 10.
mistakes.C: Step 2: n − 2 = 11 − 2 = 9 triangles, not 8. Check the subtraction.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows the exterior angles of a pentagon. Find x.
questions.explanation: Exterior angles of any convex polygon add to 360°, so x = 360 − (60 + 85 + 70 + 90) = 360 − 305 = 55. 235 uses the interior sum of 540° by mistake.
steps: The exterior angles of a convex polygon add to 360°.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 125° is the interior angle at that corner. x is the exterior angle.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 305 is the total of the four known exterior angles. Subtract it from 360.
mistakes.D: Step 1: exterior angles add to 360°. 540° is the INTERIOR angle sum of a pentagon.

questions.diagram_alt: Pentagon ABCDE with each side extended. The exterior angles are 60° at A, 85° at B, 70° at C, 90° at D and x at E

questions.prompt: AB ∥ CD and the line bends at E, as shown. ∠ABE = 41° and ∠BED = 108°. Find ∠CDE.
questions.explanation: Drawing a line through E parallel to AB shows the tip angle equals the sum of the arm angles: 108 = 41 + ∠CDE, so ∠CDE = 67°. 149° adds instead of subtracting.
steps: Draw a line through E parallel to AB and CD: it splits the tip into two alternate angles.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the tip angle is the SUM of the arm angles, so subtract 41 from 108 — do not add.
mistakes.B: Step 1: the tip angle is not split into two equal halves. The parts match the two arm angles.
mistakes.D: Step 1: ∠CDE is not linked to ∠ABE by a straight line. Use the arrowhead rule with the tip angle.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines AB and CD with a line bending at E between them, like an arrowhead pointing right. Angle ABE is 41°, the tip angle BED is 108°, and angle CDE is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: The angles of the triangle in the diagram are 2k°, 3k° and 7k° (in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7). Find the largest angle.
questions.explanation: There are 2 + 3 + 7 = 12 parts sharing 180°, so one part is 15° and the largest angle is 7 × 15 = 105°. 210° comes from sharing 360° instead of 180°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 15 is the value of k (one part). Multiply by 7 for the largest angle.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 30° is the smallest angle (2 parts). The largest has 7 parts.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the angles of a triangle add to 180°, not 360°.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with angle A = 2k°, angle B = 3k° and angle C = 7k°

questions.prompt: ABCD is an isosceles trapezium with AB ∥ DC and AD = BC. ∠ADC = (3x + 5)° and ∠BCD = (4x − 20)°. Find ∠DAB.
questions.explanation: In an isosceles trapezium the base angles are equal: 3x + 5 = 4x − 20, so x = 25 and ∠ADC = 80°. ∠DAB is co-interior with ∠ADC (AB ∥ DC), so ∠DAB = 180 − 80 = 100°. 80° is ∠ADC, not ∠DAB.
steps: AD = BC, so the base angles at D and C are equal: 3x + 5 = 4x − 20, which gives x = 25.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 80° is ∠ADC. ∠DAB is co-interior with it, so subtract from 180°.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 25 is the value of x. Substitute it back to find the angles.
mistakes.D: Step 3: ∠DAB and ∠ADC are co-interior — they add to 180°, so ∠DAB is not 2 × 80°.

questions.diagram_alt: Isosceles trapezium ABCD with AB parallel to DC and AD = BC. Angle ADC is (3x + 5)°, angle BCD is (4x − 20)°, and angle DAB is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a regular polygon with 15 sides. Find the size of each interior angle.
questions.explanation: The angle sum is (15 − 2) × 180 = 2340°, and the 15 angles are equal, so each is 2340 ÷ 15 = 156°. 24° is the exterior angle.
steps: The polygon is regular, so all 15 angles are equal.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 24° is the exterior angle (360 ÷ 15). The interior angle is 180° minus it.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 2340° is the sum of all 15 angles. Divide by 15 to share it equally.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the angle sum uses n − 2 = 13 triangles, not n − 1 = 14.

questions.diagram_alt: A regular polygon with 15 equal sides; one interior angle is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 20°. Find the sum of its interior angles.
questions.explanation: n = 360 ÷ 20 = 18 sides, so the interior angle sum is (18 − 2) × 180 = 2880°. 3240° uses 18 triangles instead of 16.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the interior angle sum uses n − 2 = 16 triangles, not n = 18.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 160° is ONE interior angle. The question asks for the sum of all of them.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 360° is the sum of the EXTERIOR angles. The interior sum is (n − 2) × 180°.

questions.prompt: AB ∥ CD. In the diagram, ∠APQ = (3x − 10)° and ∠PQD = (x + 50)°. Find ∠BPQ.
questions.explanation: ∠APQ and ∠PQD are alternate, so 3x − 10 = x + 50, giving x = 30 and ∠APQ = 80°. ∠BPQ is on a straight line with it: 180 − 80 = 100°. 80° is ∠APQ, not the angle asked for.
steps: ∠APQ and ∠PQD are alternate angles, so they are equal: 3x − 10 = x + 50.
Subtract x and add 10 to both sides: 2x = 60, so x = 30 and ∠APQ = 3 × 30 − 10 = 80°.
Angles on the straight line AB: ∠BPQ = 180 − 80 = 100°.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 80° is ∠APQ. ∠BPQ is next to it on the straight line AB, so subtract from 180°.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 30 is the value of x, not an angle. Substitute it back.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 2x = 60 is not finished — divide by 2 to get x, then find the angles.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines AB and CD cut by a transversal at P and Q. Angle APQ is (3x − 10)°, angle PQD is (x + 50)°, and angle BPQ is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: In the diagram, D is on BC, AD = BD = AC and ∠ABC = 36°. Find ∠BAC.
questions.explanation: AD = BD gives ∠BAD = 36°, so the exterior angle ∠ADC = 36 + 36 = 72°. AD = AC gives ∠ACD = 72° too, so ∠DAC = 180 − 144 = 36°. ∠BAC = 36 + 36 = 72°. 36° is only part of ∠BAC.
steps: AD = BD, so triangle ABD is isosceles: ∠BAD = ∠ABD = 36°, and the exterior angle ∠ADC = 36 + 36 = 72°.
AD = AC, so in triangle ADC, ∠ACD = ∠ADC = 72°, and ∠DAC = 180 − 72 − 72 = 36°.

mistakes.C: Step 1: 108° is ∠ADB. Keep going: use the straight line BC and triangle ADC.
mistakes.D: Step 3: triangle ABC is not isosceles with apex 72°. Use AD = AC in triangle ADC instead.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with point D on BC and segment AD. BD, AD and AC each have one dash (equal). Angle ABC is 36° and angle BAC is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: ABCD is a rhombus whose diagonals meet at O. ∠OAB = (2x + 4)° and ∠OBA = (3x + 11)°. Find ∠ABC.
questions.explanation: The diagonals of a rhombus meet at 90°, so (2x + 4) + (3x + 11) = 90, giving x = 15 and ∠OBA = 56°. The diagonal halves ∠ABC, so ∠ABC = 2 × 56 = 112°. 56° is only half of it.
steps: The diagonals of a rhombus cross at 90°, so in triangle AOB: (2x + 4) + (3x + 11) + 90 = 180, so 5x + 15 = 90.
Diagonal BD cuts ∠ABC in half, so ∠ABC = 2 × 56 = 112° (check: ∠BAD = 2 × 34 = 68 and 68 + 112 = 180 ✓).

mistakes.A: Step 3: 56° is ∠OBA, only half of ∠ABC. The diagonal BD cuts ∠ABC in half.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 68° is ∠BAD (2 × 34°). ∠ABC is at B, so double ∠OBA instead.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 15 is the value of x. Substitute it back to find the angles.

questions.diagram_alt: Rhombus ABCD with diagonals meeting at O. Angle OAB is (2x + 4)°, angle OBA is (3x + 11)°, and the diagonals cross at a right angle

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a hexagon's exterior angles: 50°, 2x°, 70°, x°, 45° and (x + 15)°. Find the LARGEST interior angle of the hexagon.
questions.explanation: The exterior angles add to 360°: 4x + 180 = 360, so x = 45. The smallest exterior angle is 45°, so the largest interior angle is 180 − 45 = 135°. 90° is the largest exterior angle, the opposite of what is asked.
steps: Exterior angles add to 360°: 50 + 2x + 70 + x + 45 + x + 15 = 360, so 4x + 180 = 360.
4x = 180, so x = 45. The exterior angles are 50°, 90°, 70°, 45°, 45° and 60°.
Interior = 180 − exterior, so the largest interior angle is next to the smallest exterior angle: 180 − 45 = 135°.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 90° is the largest EXTERIOR angle (2x). The largest interior angle sits next to the smallest exterior angle.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 45 is x, an exterior angle. Change it to an interior angle: 180 − 45.
mistakes.D: Step 3: the smallest exterior angle is 45°, not 50°. Find x first, then compare all six.

questions.diagram_alt: Hexagon ABCDEF with each side extended. The exterior angles are 50° at A, 2x° at B, 70° at C, x° at D, 45° at E and (x + 15)° at F

questions.prompt: ABCD is a square. Triangle CDE is equilateral and lies outside the square, as shown. Find ∠AEB.
questions.explanation: DE = DC = DA, so triangle ADE is isosceles with ∠ADE = 90 + 60 = 150° and ∠DEA = (180 − 150) ÷ 2 = 15°. By symmetry ∠CEB = 15°, so ∠AEB = 60 − 15 − 15 = 30°. 15° is only ∠DEA.
steps: DE = DC (equilateral) and DC = DA (square), so DE = DA and triangle ADE is isosceles. ∠ADE = 90 + 60 = 150°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 15° is ∠DEA. ∠AEB is what is left of the 60° angle at E after removing ∠DEA and ∠CEB.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 60° is the whole angle ∠DEC. Lines EA and EB cut off 15° on each side.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 150° is ∠ADE (90 + 60). It is at D, not at E.

questions.diagram_alt: Square ABCD with equilateral triangle CDE on top of side DC, outside the square. Lines AE and BE are drawn and angle AEB is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: A polygon has one interior angle of 120°, and every other interior angle is 150°. How many sides does it have?
questions.explanation: The angle sum is (n − 2) × 180, and it also equals 150(n − 1) + 120. So 180n − 360 = 150n − 30, giving 30n = 330 and n = 11. 12 ignores the one 120° angle.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 12 is the regular polygon with ALL angles 150°. Here one angle is 120°, so write (n − 2) × 180 = 150(n − 1) + 120.
mistakes.B: Step 1: there are n − 1 angles of 150°, not n. Use 150(n − 1) + 120.
mistakes.C: Step 2: check the signs: 180n − 360 = 150n − 30 gives 30n = 330, not 390.
